teaser: A painting that celebrates flight, with no airplane anywhere in it.
review_notes:
Identification of the two men as the artist and his brother Henri, director of the Nieuport aircraft company (per MoMA).
Setting possibly Meulan, a sailing center on the Seine: stated as 'thought to be'.
Shown at the Salon d'Automne of 1913.
MoMA acquisition in 1947.
Dimensions 235.9 x 195.6 cm.
Wilbur Wright's 1908 demonstration flights near Le Mans, the artist's birthplace.
Which of the two seated men is which brother is not stated in the lesson on purpose.

lesson.text: In 1914, Robert Delaunay painted Homage to Blériot, a canvas crowded with propellers, biplanes and spinning discs. Decades later, posters of rockets would cheer the space race in much the same excited way. Roger de La Fresnaye celebrated flight a year before Delaunay, and he did it with two men at a table.

The canvas is big: about 236 by 196 centimeters, close to 8 feet tall. The two men are larger than life. They sit outdoors, leaning toward each other over a bare table, and around them the world seems to have come loose. Roofs, clouds and a flag hang in the blue like cut paper.

They are thought to be the painter and his brother Henri. That matters, because Henri de La Fresnaye ran the Nieuport company, one of the French firms that built airplanes. This is a family conversation about the most exciting business of the day.
Roger de La Fresnaye was born in Le Mans. In 1908, when he was 23, Wilbur Wright chose a racecourse outside that same town for the demonstration flights that convinced Europe the airplane was real.
So where is the airplane? You can search every corner: there is none. The title promises a conquest, and the picture gives you older, gentler ways of riding the wind instead.
One thing in this picture actually flies. It is small. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The balloon
spots.text: A single golden balloon drifts high at upper left. France had been proud of balloons since the Montgolfier brothers launched the first ones in 1783. The dream of flight starts here.

lesson.text: The balloon is the past. The brothers at the table are planning the future. Between them, La Fresnaye places two more objects pushed by moving air, and together they turn the canvas into a short history of wind.

lesson.title: Carried by air
lesson.text: Three objects, three ways the wind works for people.

spots.title: The sail
spots.text: A white sailboat sits on the horizon at the right. The setting may be Meulan, a sailing spot on the Seine. A sail is the oldest machine for catching air.

spots.title: The flag
spots.text: A huge French tricolor floats in the sky, attached to nothing. Its blue, white and red spread across the whole painting. Conquering the air was a matter of national pride.

spots.title: The clouds
spots.text: The clouds are built from overlapping white discs, as solid as balls of plaster. La Fresnaye gives the sky a geometry, as if it could be measured and mapped.

lesson.text: Notice what the flag does to the color. Before 1912, Cubist pictures were mostly brown and gray. La Fresnaye had seen the bright canvases of Delaunay, who thought color itself could build a picture, and he floods his scene with clear blue, red, white and orange.
La Fresnaye borrowed the Cubist habit of breaking the world into flat planes, but kept his figures whole and readable. It is a gentle Cubism, easy to enter.

The men show this best. Their bodies are simplified into blocks, yet you never doubt where an arm or a knee is. And the space around them ignores gravity. A village that should sit far below on the ground floats at the height of their heads.

spots.title: The thinker
spots.text: The man on the left rests his chin on his fist, eyes lowered. His face is a few flat patches of ochre and white. He listens, or calculates.

spots.title: The man in profile
spots.text: His companion sits upright in strict profile, like a face on a coin. An orange jacket makes him the warmest shape on the canvas.

spots.title: Floating roofs
spots.text: Pink and gray rooftops tumble through the gap between the two heads. Seen from an aircraft, a village looks just like this: small, tilted, toy-like.

spots.title: The bare table
spots.text: The tabletop tips toward you so that you see its whole surface, a favorite Cubist trick. There are no plans or drawings on it. The idea is still only in the air.

spots.title: A village below
spots.text: At lower left, more houses and treetops appear as if seen from high above. The brothers seem to sit on top of the landscape instead of in it.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: “R. de La Fresnaye 13.” The date is 1913, four years after Louis Blériot became the first person to fly an airplane across the English Channel.

lesson.text: Blériot's 1909 Channel crossing took about 37 minutes and made him a national hero overnight. Within a few years, French factories such as Nieuport were among the busiest aircraft builders in the world.

The optimism did not last. In 1914 the war began, and the airplane became a weapon. La Fresnaye volunteered for the army, although his health was fragile. He came back with ruined lungs and never painted on this scale again.
He died of tuberculosis in 1925, at the age of 40. The Conquest of the Air crossed the Atlantic afterwards and entered the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1947.
Seen from today, the title sounds almost innocent. In 1913 you could still paint the conquest of the air as two brothers, a flag and a fine afternoon of wind.

quiz.question: Which flying machine appears in the painting?
quiz.explanation: Only a small golden balloon drifts in the upper left; there is no airplane.

quiz.question: Why does it matter that one of the men is thought to be Henri de La Fresnaye?
options: He ran the Nieuport aircraft company
quiz.explanation: The painter's brother directed a firm that built airplanes.

quiz.question: What did La Fresnaye take from Robert Delaunay?
quiz.explanation: Delaunay believed color could build a picture, and La Fresnaye brightened his palette.

quiz.question: What are the clouds made of in this picture?
quiz.explanation: The clouds are solid-looking white circles.

quiz.question: What happened to La Fresnaye after 1914?
options: The war ruined his lungs and he died at 40
quiz.explanation: He volunteered, came back ill and died of tuberculosis in 1925.

facts.text: A large airplane crosses the sky at the top of the painting.
facts.explanation: There is no airplane at all, only a balloon, a sailboat and a flag.

facts.text: The French flag in the picture floats in the sky without a pole.
facts.explanation: The tricolor hangs in the blue, attached to nothing.

facts.text: La Fresnaye was born in Le Mans, where Wilbur Wright flew in 1908.
facts.explanation: Wright's demonstration flights took place outside the painter's home town.
